summary: Zechariah 11 (17 verses) continues the story of temple, Messiah, return. Starting with 'Open your doors, Lebanon, that the fire may devour your cedars.', it moves through themes of temple, Messiah, return and calls readers toward temple, Messiah, return.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows temple, Messiah, return lived out in post-exile jerusalem. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: Open your doors, Lebanon, that the fire may devour your cedars.
Then I said, “I will not feed you. That which dies, let it die; and that which is to be cut off, let it be cut off; and let those who are left eat each other’s flesh.”
Woe to the worthless shepherd who leaves the flock! The sword will strike his arm and his right eye. His arm will be completely withered, and his right eye will be totally blinded!”

questions.question: What is happening in Zechariah 11?
questions.answer: In 17 verses, this chapter zechariah 11 (17 verses) continues the story of temple, messiah, return. starting with 'open your doors, lebanon, that the fire may devour your cedars.', it moves through themes of temple, messiah, return and calls readers toward temple, messiah, return. The setting is post-exile jerusalem, written to returnees. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Zechariah and why 11 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally zechariah, addressed to returnees around ~520-470 bc. This chapter fits the book's purpose as visions + oracles — its themes of temple, Messiah, return build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'covenant' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: Binding promise/agreement God makes with people. In this chapter, it appears in context of temple, Messiah, return. For a first-time reader: think of it as binding promise/agreement god makes with people, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through temple, Messiah, return and faith, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 16 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'For, behold, I will raise up a shepherd in the land who will not visit those who are cut off, neither will seek those who are scattered, nor heal that which is broken, nor feed tha...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about temple, Messiah, return. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
